seoDescription: Learn how to set up a Spring Boot WebFlux project and dive into the internal workflow of Project Reactor's Mono and Flux publishers. This tutorial guides you through creating a reactive application from scratch using the Spring Initializr in IntelliJ. You'll see practical demonstrations of how to create Mono and Flux streams, subscribe to them, and use the `.log()` operator to observe the underlying Reactive Streams events like onSubscribe, request, onNext, and onComplete.

chapters.title: Introduction and Project Setup
chapters.description: The video begins by outlining the goal of exploring Mono and Flux and then walks through creating a new Spring Boot reactive project in IntelliJ.

chapters.title: Examining Project Dependencies
chapters.description: This chapter reviews the `pom.xml` file, highlighting the `spring-boot-starter-webflux` and `reactor-test` dependencies added to the project.

chapters.title: Creating a Mono Test Case
chapters.description: A test case for Mono is created to demonstrate how to instantiate a Mono publisher, which can handle a single data element.

chapters.title: Subscribing to a Mono and Initial Run
chapters.description: This section explains that Mono and Flux act as publishers and shows how a subscriber must call the `subscribe` method to receive data.

chapters.title: Logging the Reactive Stream Workflow
chapters.description: The `.log()` operator is introduced to inspect the sequence of events and verify that the Mono's execution follows the Reactive Streams specification.

chapters.title: Simulating and Handling Mono Errors
chapters.description: An error is intentionally introduced into the Mono stream using `Mono.error()` to demonstrate the `onError` termination event and how to handle it.

chapters.title: Creating a Flux Test Case
chapters.description: Attention shifts to Flux, demonstrating how to create a publisher that can emit multiple data elements using `Flux.just()`.

chapters.title: Logging the Flux Workflow and Concatenation
chapters.description: The `.log()` operator is used again, this time on a Flux, to show multiple `onNext` events, and `concatWith()` is used to add more elements to the stream.

chapters.title: Simulating Flux Errors and Final Recap
chapters.description: An error is introduced mid-stream into the Flux to prove that the stream terminates at the point of error, and the complete Reactive Streams workflow is recapped.

summary:
## Project Setup
To begin working with Spring WebFlux, you create a Spring Boot project and include a key dependency:

- **Dependency**: `spring-boot-starter-webflux`
- This starter transitively includes `reactor-core`, which provides the Mono and Flux APIs.
- The demonstration uses a JUnit test class (`MonoFluxTest`) to explore reactive concepts without needing to build a full API.

## Understanding Publishers: Mono and Flux
Project Reactor provides two core `Publisher` types for handling asynchronous data streams:

- **`Mono<T>`**: Represents a stream of **0 or 1** items. It's used for asynchronous operations that will yield a single result or no result at all.
  - Example: `Mono<String> monoString = Mono.just("javateki");`

- **`Flux<T>`**: Represents a stream of **0 to N** items. It's used for handling sequences of multiple data elements.
  - Example: `Flux<String> fluxString = Flux.just("Spring", "Spring Boot", "Hibernate");`

> [!NOTE]
> Both `Mono` and `Flux` are lazy. Nothing happens until a `Subscriber` subscribes to the stream.

## The Reactive Streams Workflow
The interaction between a `Publisher` (Mono/Flux) and a `Subscriber` follows a strict protocol defined by the Reactive Streams specification:

1.  **Subscription**: The process begins when a `Subscriber` calls the `.subscribe()` method on a `Publisher`.
2.  **`onSubscribe`**: The `Publisher` responds by calling the `onSubscribe(Subscription subscription)` method on the `Subscriber`. This passes a `Subscription` object, establishing the connection.
3.  **`request(n)`**: The `Subscriber` uses the `Subscription` object to request a number of items (`n`) from the `Publisher`. This implements backpressure.
4.  **`onNext(T t)`**: The `Publisher` sends data items to the `Subscriber` by calling `onNext` for each item, up to the number requested.
5.  **Termination**: The stream completes in one of two ways:
    *   **`onComplete()`**: Called by the `Publisher` to signal that all data has been sent successfully.
    *   **`onError(Throwable t)`**: Called by the `Publisher` if an error occurs during processing.

## Verifying the Workflow with `.log()`
A powerful tool for observing the internal events of a reactive stream is the `.log()` operator.

- Placing `.log()` in a reactive chain prints every signal (onSubscribe, request, onNext, onComplete, onError) to the console.
- This makes it an invaluable debugging tool for visualizing the flow of data and events.

```java
// Example: Logging a Mono stream
Mono.just("javateki")
    .log()
    .subscribe(System.out::println);
```

## Error Handling
Error handling is a critical part of the reactive contract.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Once an `onError` signal is emitted, the stream is terminated. No further `onNext` or `onComplete` events will be sent, even if there are more operators or data sources chained after the error.

- An error can be introduced into a stream using `Mono.error(new Exception())` or `Flux.error(new Exception())`.
- The `.subscribe()` method can be overloaded to handle these error signals gracefully.

```java
// Example: Subscribing with an error handler
fluxString
    .log()
    .subscribe(
        data -> System.out.println("Received: " + data),
        error -> System.err.println("Error: " + error.getMessage())
    );
```
